e.t: This adjective describes a person who is doing good—actively acting in a beneficial or morally good way. It presents goodness as something expressed through conduct, not merely held as an inward quality. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, the word occurs once, in Sirach 42:14. The reference identifies its occurrence, but the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense remains a description of someone characterized by good action.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Addamin” or “Aththamin,” rather than a general term describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament translation. The word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:7. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be explained further; its supported lexical function is simply a proper name.

This noun means “freedom from fear”—a condition in which a person is not held back or troubled by fear. It expresses security or confidence rather than fearfulness itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) writings represented here, the word occurs three times, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains release from fear and the resulting freedom to act without dread.

Ainagalim, also rendered Enagalim, is a proper name for a specific place. It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but a name used to identify a location. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezekiel 47:10. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in that passage cannot be stated beyond its role as a place name. The two forms, “Ainagalim” and “Enagalim,” identify the same named place in this lexical entry.

This Greek LXX verb means “grind” or “bruise,” describing the act of crushing or breaking something through pressure. It functions as an action word rather than naming an object or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 47:2, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s basic sense points to physically working something down, crushing it, or causing it to become bruised.

This verb means to “proclaim publicly”—to announce something openly so that others can hear it. It describes a public act of declaring or making something known, rather than a private thought or quiet conversation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains an open, public proclamation.

This adjective means “unworthy,” describing someone or something that does not merit a given honor, place, treatment, or consideration. It identifies a lack of deserving value in relation to what is being discussed. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including in Esther, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This verb means “speak against”: it describes verbally opposing or contradicting what another person has said. As a verb, it focuses on the act of answering with disagreement rather than merely being present or remaining silent. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 12 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion, with additional use in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means “sit apart,” describing someone remaining separate or withdrawn from others. It is used in the Greek Old Testament to express physical separation rather than movement toward or among people. The word occurs eight times across eight verses in this corpus, including passages from Leviticus, Isaiah, Lamentations, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains sitting separately or staying apart.

This LXX verb means “nip off”—to cut, pinch, or remove a small part from something. It describes an action of taking away a portion rather than removing the whole object. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in this corpus, including passages in Leviticus, 1 Samuel, 2 Kings, Ezekiel, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being removed, but its basic idea remains a small cutting or separation.

This word means “chief of a tribe.” It can name a tribal leader or describe someone in that leadership role, functioning as either a noun or an adjective. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy 29:9 and Joshua 21:1. Its basic focus is a person identified by authority within a tribe. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “stork,” referring to the large bird known by that name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Jeremiah. The word identifies the bird itself rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This Greek LXX adjective means “disorderly,” describing someone or something that lacks proper order or behaves in an unruly way. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action, person, or object by itself. In the LXX Greek corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 1:19. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a departure from order, proper arrangement, or disciplined conduct.

This noun means “nonsense”—speech, thinking, or conduct regarded as lacking sound sense. It identifies what is foolish or unreasonable rather than expressing a person, place, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures, it occurs 33 times, including passages in Deuteronomy, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a clear description of senseless or unreasonable thought or behavior.

Bazan, also rendered Vazan, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 1:10. The available lexical information identifies it simply as the name Bazan or Vazan; without the surrounding verse text, its particular role in that passage cannot be explained further. Its meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it names a person or figure mentioned in the Esther account.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Besemiin” or “Vesemin,” rather than a common term describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 19:33. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to a particular named entity rather than expressing a general idea. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what entity the name identifies there.

This noun means “blasphemy” or “defamation”: speech that dishonors, insults, or falsely attacks someone, especially in a way that treats what is holy with contempt. Its central idea is disgraceful, injurious speech rather than an ordinary disagreement. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs five times, in Ezekiel and 1–2 Maccabees. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic meaning remains verbal dishonor or slander.

This Greek LXX noun means “infant,” referring to a very young child. It identifies a child at the earliest stage of life, rather than an older child or adult. The word occurs five times in the supplied Greek LXX corpus, appearing once each in Sirach and 1–4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a young infant.

This word means “4” and is also identified as “daleth.” It functions as an indeclinable number, so its basic role is to mark the quantity four rather than describe an action, person, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 58 times across 57 verses, in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its repeated use in different books confirms a consistent numerical sense, while the precise thing counted is determined by the surrounding verse.

This verb means “protest”: to speak or act in objection. It describes the act of making a protest rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 30 times across 29 verses, from Exodus through Malachi. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains an expressed objection.

This verb means to “sow abroad” or “scatter around,” describing the act of spreading people or things apart. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for scattering, including the dispersal of people among different places. The word occurs 63 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion. Its central idea remains purposeful or consequential spreading rather than keeping something gathered in one place.

This verb means to fill something up by weaving. It describes completing or making a woven surface through the act of interlacing threads, rather than merely adding material in a general sense. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Exodus 36:30. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the completion of something by weaving it together.

This adjective describes what is possible or what someone is able to do. It can identify an action, outcome, or capability as within reach rather than impossible. In the Greek Old Testament and related books represented by the LXX corpus, it occurs 160 times, showing that this is a broadly used word for ability or possibility. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the person, action, or circumstance being described.

This verb describes having fortitude and controlling oneself. It refers to inner strength expressed through restraint: a person does not simply react, but exercises self-control. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, showing a focused use rather than a broad, frequently repeated term. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains disciplined strength under control.

This verb means “get.” It describes the action of getting something and functions as an action word in a sentence. Its precise sense in a particular passage depends on what is being gotten and the surrounding words. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah 4:29 and once in 1 Maccabees 6:46. These references show its limited occurrence in this corpus, while the basic meaning remains the action of getting.

This adjective describes something that is evident—plainly visible, recognizable, or clear rather than hidden or uncertain. It functions as a straightforward description of a person, thing, fact, or situation whose reality can be readily perceived. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains the same: something unmistakably clear or evident.

This verb means to be “full of amazement” or “astonished.” It describes a person who is deeply surprised or overwhelmed with wonder. As a verb, it expresses the experience of becoming or being astonished rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 30:9. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “uproot”: to pull something out by its roots, removing it from its place. It can describe the decisive removal of a plant or, figuratively, the taking away of something established. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages in Judges, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Zephaniah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being removed and the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “diminish”: to make something less, lower its extent, or reduce its amount. It describes an action or change rather than a person, object, or fixed quality. The word appears 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, including Numbers, Samuel, Psalms, Ezekiel, Daniel, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being reduced and the surrounding sentence.

Elimuth is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 12:21. The available wording preserves the name as “Elimuth,” also represented as “Elimouth,” rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the person’s role and the significance of the reference cannot be explained from this word alone.

This verb means to calumniate: to speak against someone in a damaging or accusatory way. It describes an act of verbal attack rather than a physical action. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs six times, once in Numbers and five times in Psalms. The basic idea is a hostile accusation or denunciation; the surrounding verse determines who is speaking and whom the charge targets.

This Greek LXX adjective means “valued” or “valuable,” describing someone or something regarded as precious, worthy, or held in esteem. It can describe people, possessions, or things considered important rather than ordinary or insignificant. The word occurs 26 times in the Greek LXX corpus, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that it serves this broad sense across different settings. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing is being described.

This noun means “dreamer,” referring to a person associated with dreams. It identifies someone by this characteristic rather than describing an action or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 37:19. The word’s basic sense is therefore straightforward: a dreamer is a person known or recognized for dreaming. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical meaning remains centered on a person connected with dreams.

This noun means “re-existence”: existence again or renewed existence. It names the idea of coming into existence once more, rather than simply continuing in the same state. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 7:4. The word’s exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation context, but its basic lexical meaning is the return to existence or renewed existence.

This Greek LXX noun means “surname,” an additional name used to identify a person beyond the person’s primary name. It refers to a naming designation rather than an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. The precise significance of the surname in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX verb means “fling on”: to throw or cast something onto a person or surface. It describes a forceful placing or throwing action rather than a quiet setting down. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 13 verses. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what is being thrown and what receives it, but its central idea remains the sudden or forceful act of flinging something on.

This Greek LXX noun refers to someone “born in the seventh month.” It identifies a person according to the month of birth, rather than expressing an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel 39, appearing in verses 12 and 14. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains focused on birth taking place in the seventh month.

This adjective describes someone who is held in good regard—“in good repute” or “honoured.” It points to recognized standing or a favorable reputation rather than merely describing a private feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 3:5. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise person or situation it describes must be understood from that context. Its central idea remains clear: the person or group called by this word is regarded favorably and treated as worthy of honor.

This adjective means “pretty,” describing someone or something as pleasing in appearance. It is a straightforward descriptive word rather than a title, action, or inner quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 12:11. The word therefore identifies outward attractiveness, while the surrounding verse and passage determine how that description functions in context. Its precise force in Genesis 12:11 must be understood from the verse itself and the events surrounding it.

This Greek LXX verb means “have a bouquet,” describing something that gives off a fragrant or pleasant scent. It refers to possessing or bearing an appealing fragrance rather than merely naming a flower or perfume. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Zechariah and once in Sirach, showing its use across both biblical and deuterocanonical Greek writings. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is having a pleasing bouquet or fragrance.

This word means “gentleness,” describing a mild, considerate quality rather than harshness or severity. It is a noun, so it names this quality as something recognized or expressed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:13. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense remains gentleness: a manner marked by softness, restraint, and kindness rather than forceful severity.

This adjective means “established by God.” It describes something as having its standing established by God rather than merely being arranged or recognized by human authority. Its central idea is divine establishment. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 6:23. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage depends on the sentence and wider context.

The word is the proper name “Thergama.” It functions as a name rather than as a description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel: Ezekiel 27:14 and Ezekiel 38:6. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional ordinary-language definition, so its precise identity or reference must be understood from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This word means “noise; uproar,” referring to a loud, disorderly disturbance or commotion. As a noun, it names the sound or public tumult itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 11 times, showing a recurring word for disruptive noise or unrest. Its uses span books such as Ezra, Esther, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, but the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iediēl” or “Iethil.” It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: 5:24 and 11:45. Since no broader definition or contextual verse text is provided, its ordinary function is simply to name an individual. The exact person intended in either passage must be determined from the surrounding biblical context.

Iezrael is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the named entity called Iezrael rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word appears 29 times across 24 Old Testament verses, from Joshua through Hosea. Because the available information provides the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific reference—such as whether it identifies a person or a place—must be determined from the passage where it occurs.

Iouri, also rendered Iuri, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies one individual in the genealogy recorded at 1 Chronicles 5:14. Because it occurs only once in this corpus and no verse text is provided here, its role is limited to identifying that person; the name itself does not supply a broader teaching or concept.

Kaath is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader abstract meaning. The name occurs 44 times across 40 verses, from Genesis 46:11 through 2 Chronicles 34:12, with many occurrences in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a personal name.

Kalita is a proper name, meaning the word functions as the personal designation “Kalita.” In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) data, it appears once, at Nehemiah 10:11. Since no verse text or wider context is provided here, the name itself does not supply a further description of the person or the role associated with that occurrence. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “smoke” or “smolder”: it describes producing smoke or continuing to burn without a clear flame. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for something visibly giving off smoke, whether from fire or another burning source. The word occurs eight times in the LXX corpus, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is burning and how the surrounding passage describes it.

This Greek LXX noun means “devouring,” referring to the act of consuming something eagerly or completely. It names an act rather than a person or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 31:15; the surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how the word functions there. Its central idea remains the consuming or eating away of something, expressed as an action or process.

This verb means to “left behind” or “forsake.” It describes the act of leaving someone or something behind rather than remaining with or continuing alongside it. As a verb, it expresses an action, not a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 28:9. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning is the act of abandoning or leaving behind.

This adjective describes something as “irrigated” or “watered”—made moist or supplied with water. It identifies a condition rather than an action, telling the reader what something is like. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:16. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what it describes there, but its basic meaning remains something receiving or having water.

This verb means “abuse”: to use or treat someone or something wrongly, harshly, or beyond what is proper. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is being abused in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, showing a specific but repeated action-word meaning rather than a broad descriptive term.

This word means “behind” or “after,” describing a position at the back of something or a place later in a sequence. As an adverb or preposition, it can indicate following someone, being located behind them, or coming afterward. Its basic sense remains consistent across the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, where it occurs 23 times in the LXX corpus. The surrounding words determine whether the emphasis is physical location or order in time.

This verb means to become stained or soiled. It describes something marked, dirtied, or made impure by contact with something unclean. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 11:33, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic sense remains straightforward: it portrays the condition of being defiled rather than clean. As a verb, it expresses an action or resulting state—something becoming marked or dirty.

This noun means “shipmaster” or “pilot”—the person responsible for guiding and directing a vessel. It refers to someone with practical control of a ship’s course, not merely a passenger or sailor. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including three references in Ezekiel’s description of maritime activity. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears: a person who steers or manages a ship.

This Greek Septuagint verb means to “rush out” or to be “eager.” It describes energetic movement or a ready, urgent disposition rather than a quiet or hesitant response. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament represented by this corpus, in Job 38:8 and Jeremiah 4:19. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains swift action or eager movement.

μαρτυρέω means to testify or attest—to give a confirming witness or statement about something. As a verb, it describes the act of bearing testimony rather than the testimony itself. In this Greek LXX corpus, it appears 13 times. The word can describe a person speaking as a witness or affirming what is known to be true. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being affirmed and who is giving the testimony.

This Greek LXX verb means to “sing” or “chant”—to express words in a sung or rhythmic way. It describes the act of vocal musical expression rather than naming a song or a singer. In this corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 18:15. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of singing or chanting.

This word describes an associate or partaker—someone who shares in a person, group, activity, or benefit. As a noun, it can identify such a companion; as an adjective, it characterizes someone as sharing or participating. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears seven times, including passages from 1 Samuel, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Hosea, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on what the person is associated with or shares in there.

This noun means “smallness,” “littleness,” or “meanness”—the quality of being small, slight, or low in importance. It can describe limited size or a diminished condition rather than greatness or prominence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 12. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and larger context, but its central idea remains something regarded as small, little, or mean.

e.h: A Word for Ten Thousand Times
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “ten thousand times”. It expresses a ten-thousandfold amount or repetition, functioning as an adverb to describe how greatly or how many times something occurs. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, in Sirach 23:19. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains multiplication on a very large scale.

This word means “sanctuary,” referring to a holy place set apart for worship and the presence of God. It is a noun used for a sacred building or designated holy space, especially in descriptions of Israel’s worship and temple furnishings. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 93 times, showing that it is a regular term for sacred places rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “wedding,” referring to the marriage celebration or ceremony. It is a noun, so it names the event rather than describing an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Song of Songs 3:11. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the wedding itself. This meaning is distinct from words for the bride, groom, or marriage partners.

Yellow describes a yellow color or appearance. It is an adjective, so it identifies something by its visible color rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Leviticus 13:36. Its precise application there depends on the wording and surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a description of yellow coloring. The word therefore serves as a straightforward color term within the passage.

Ozi is a personal name, referring to people identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common noun describing an object, action, or quality. The name occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in genealogical and historical records, including Chronicles and Nehemiah. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition or verse text, its specific significance belongs to the individual and context in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “appoint” or “mark out.” It describes setting something or someone apart by an established decision or boundary. The word can therefore refer either to assigning a role or to determining a limit. It occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including passages in Numbers, Joshua, Proverbs, Daniel, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being appointed or marked out there.

This adjective describes something happening or being accompanied by “with a fair wind”—that is, under favorable wind conditions. It refers to a wind that helps rather than hinders movement. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 59:5, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains a favorable wind or a condition aided by such wind.

This noun means an exhortation or an address: words spoken to encourage, urge, or counsel someone. It refers to a form of purposeful speech rather than a physical object or personal quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 8:9. The reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse is needed to determine the precise force of the address in that passage.

This adjective describes something that surrounds a person or thing on every side, leaving no direction uncovered. It expresses complete encirclement rather than merely being nearby or touching one part. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:41. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is being enclosed or surrounded completely.

This adjective means “of clay,” describing something made from or associated with clay. It identifies a material that is earthy, molded, and comparatively fragile rather than metallic, wooden, or stone-like. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including passages in Job, Daniel, and Bel and the Dragon. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun or object it describes, but its central meaning remains a clay material or clay-like quality.

This noun means “government,” referring to an organized civic authority or governing arrangement. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Maccabees 12:7. Because no verse text is available here, the word’s exact force in that sentence cannot be described further; its established meaning remains the governing authority or political order being discussed. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on the authority itself, its administration, or the community under its rule.

This word describes something “darkgleaming” or “dark.” It functions as a descriptive word, and may also be used as a noun for something having that quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 1:6. Its basic sense points to a visibly dark appearance or a surface that gleams with a dark tone. The surrounding verse determines exactly what object or material it describes there.

This Greek LXX verb means “die before”: it describes one person dying earlier than another person or before a specified event. It expresses precedence in death, not simply dying in general. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 4 Maccabees 13:18. Because the verse text is not provided here, the exact comparison or event involved must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Rōsai, rendered Rhose, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name appears once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 26:6. The available information establishes the name and its use as a personal designation, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain anything further about the person or the passage. Its significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding context.

Sabek is a name, preserved as “Sabek” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 22:13. Because the available information identifies the word only by this name and does not provide the verse text or surrounding context, its broader significance cannot be stated here. Its basic lexical meaning is therefore the name “Sabek,” functioning as a noun and referring to the named entity in that passage.

Salem is a proper name, referring to someone or somewhere identified by that name. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:25. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine the person, place, or significance intended in that verse; that requires the surrounding passage. Here, Salem functions as a named designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object.

Samsai, also rendered Samse, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs four times in the Greek LXX, all in Ezra chapter 4, at Ezra 4:8, 4:9, 4:17, and 4:23. The name itself gives the person’s designation, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand that person’s particular role in each occurrence.

Saul is a proper name referring to people named Saul in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It is especially associated with Saul, Israel’s king, whose name appears frequently in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel. The name is also used for other individuals, so its exact referent depends on the surrounding passage. This LXX word occurs 381 times, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion of the corpus. Its standard English rendering is “Saul.”

This noun means “sin” or “shin.” It can name either wrongdoing or the letter-name “shin,” depending on how it functions in its setting. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Psalms 118:161. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, the precise sense in that occurrence cannot be determined from the word alone. Its basic lexical range is therefore limited to these two stated meanings.

This Greek verb means “signify”: it describes expressing or indicating meaning. It is used 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, appearing across historical, prophetic, and instructional passages. The word therefore concerns the act of making something meaningful or recognizable through what is said or shown, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being signified. Its earliest listed occurrence is Exodus 18:20, and its latest is 2 Maccabees 11:17.

This Greek LXX noun means “staff,” a rod or walking stick carried or used by a person. It names a tangible object rather than an action, quality, or person.
